utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, is May 13, 2008. Good morning to the Prosecution, to the Defence counsel, to the accused, and to everyone assisting us in this case. Today we are going to proceed with the testimony of a witness called by the Prlic Defence. I understand that Mr. Karnavas wanted to take the floor, he has some preliminary remarks for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. Just a couple of technical points. First of all, there were two additional documents over the weekend while proofing the witness. We did provide everyone with copies of that. They're not in the e-court system because the system wasn't working during the weekend I'm told, and in any event that's that. And this is something that the witness provided to us when he arrived, so it wasn't something that we knew in advance. The other point, in meeting with the witness this morning very briefly just to sort of -- our habit to sort of welcome them to the court and talk to them a little bit. Two matters were brought to my attention which I thought I would share with everyone as part of the proofing process so that there's no surprise. With respect to one particular document, which is 1D 02626, 1D 02626, it's dated 12 June 1998. It's a compilation of data from 1992 to 1998. We'll hear testimony from the gentleman who will tell us that he's familiar with this document and why he's familiar, but two points that might be relevant. One is on footnote number 1 of this document it talks about elections that were held for BiH in 1996. I was told that for those refugees from BiH that were still in Croatia they were allowed to vote from Croatia for the elections in -- that were being held in BiH, that the elections were conducted by the office of the ODPR, the particular office that he had worked for, of displaced persons and refugees, and not the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That this was -- that they consciously -- there was a conscious decision not to have the embassy, but rather this particular office which was monitored at the time by OSCE, the Organization of Security and Cooperation in Europe. Everybody should be aware that they were the ones that were involved in Bosnia and Herzegovina in monitoring the elections and in organizing the elections, and that he will also say that after the elections it was Ambassador -- I believe it's Robert Frowick, I can't pronounce his name correctly but -- yes, who was at the time at the head of the OSCE who had issued a certificate of appreciation to the Croatian government for their assistance in this process. The other part that was brought to my attention in this particular report if we go to page 3, paragraph 4, page 3, paragraph 4, again sticking with the same document, 1D 02626, you will see at the second-to-last paragraph right above paragraph number 5, there is some mentioning of some events that took place in the summer of 1995 to May 1996 with respect to a particular camp in Krupcjensko [phoen]. It's my understanding that there there were large numbers of Muslim refugees that had settled among themselves, this was not an authorised camp, they had done it by themselves, that the Croatian government was being asked to dismantle this camp, the Muslims there that were under Mr. Abdic at the time refused. In any event they were able to close down the camp and relocate all those refugees to settlements in Gasinci, in Obonjan, and it was there also under the auspices of OSCE that elections were held. And of course all of this is relevant because if we reminisce back to what witness Azra Krajsek indicated that those camps were inhumane and so on and so forth, so again this is part of the testimony that the gentleman will describe the events in those camps and this is why this is relevant. I just learned of this, I pass it on, and hopefully it will not be of any traumatic inconvenience to anyone around the court to adjust themselves to this new information. I'm told that some correction needs to be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to draw the attention of the B/C/S interpreters that when Mr. Karnavas says "camp" he means a camp for campers and not a camp for detainees. This is something that might significantly affect the course of these proceedings and how they are perceived by the public following these proceedings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll have the witness brought in now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karnavas pull the microphone towards him, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Damir Zoric, the 1st of January, 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an occupation currently; and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I manage a private company in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before a court of law about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia; if that's the case, in which court did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which case, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Martinovic, Naletilic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already testified here, so my explanations will be very brief. You've been called by the Prlic Defence to testify here today. You have met Mr. Karnavas already before this hearing. In the first stage of your testimony, you will have to answer questions put to you by Mr. Karnavas. The four Judges sitting before you may at any time put follow-up questions to you, following questions put to you by Mr. Karnavas on the basis of documents we show you. Once this is over, the other Defence counsel representing the other accused will be in a position to put you questions as part of cross-examination they may decide to conduct if they think it necessary. After that, the Prosecutor, who is sitting to your right, will have as long as the Defence counsel in chief to put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. And there may be a re-examination at the end if necessary. Every hour and a half we have a 20-minute break. You are -- have been scheduled to testify until Thursday and will be sitting here from 9.00 a.m. in the morning. If at any time you feel uncomfortable, tell us immediately and I'll adjourn for a short break. This is the way we are going to proceed, and without further ado I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zoric. You're going to have to pick up because we need to pick up your voice because we will get some complaints from the translators, and rightly so. First I'm going to cover part of your background very quickly. Now, can you tell us in 1990 what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: That year I was working at the University of Zagreb, I was a young researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when did you leave that position to take up any other positions that might be relevant to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I left in August 1991 when the government of democratic unity came to power in Zagreb, and I was invited to become part of that cabinet. I was the advisor to the deputy prime minister at the time. The deputy prime minister or the vice-president was in charge of social issues, such as health and social welfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mate Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you a member of HDZ at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And have you ever been a member of HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: From 1995 to 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you were doing some research. What sort of research were you doing before you were invited to this position?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I'm a BA in history and ethnology or cultural anthropology, if you like. I also took an MA in the same field and later on I went on to a Ph.D. My research had to do with those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, focusing on your activities in Dr. Granic's office, could you please explain to us very briefly what exactly you were doing at the time, and we're speaking about 1991 as I understand it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The idea was for me to work as his assistant and to help him with the preparations for reforms to be introduced in the social sector, including the university. Unfortunately, we didn't manage to do that much because the war began. It so happened that all of us who were there at the time did most of our work dealing with the consequences of the war. In this case, people who were streaming into liberated areas from other war-torn areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Concretely what were you asked to do? Please give us the month and the year to start with so we have that as a starting point.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar, Croatia was virtually flooded with refugees. It didn't really have a civilian body that was in charge of dealing with those people. November 1991, I was approached with a proposal to try and organize, in cooperation with others, an office responsible to the cabinet that would take care of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the translation we heard "refugees." This is the fall of Vukovar, and as I understand Vukovar is in Croatia. So are we speaking about refugees or are we speaking about displaced persons or are we speaking about both?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At the time we weren't really familiar with international legal terminology, we simply had no experience in such matters. Refugees was the term we used when referring to those people or displaced persons. It wasn't before much later that we realized that there was a distinction drawn by the letter of international conventions between internally displaced citizens and refugees who crossed from one country to another. Virtually the whole of that first year we referred to all of them as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps it would be good to give us an impression as far as what was available at the time, what sort of infrastructure, what sort of resources, what sort of technical knowledge existed in the Republic of Croatia at the time of the fall of Vukovar so that we have some sort of understanding of what was available at the time because we're going to be going 1991, 1992, 1993, and onwards. So at that point could you tell us exactly what existed.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Infrastructure is perhaps too ambitious a term. There was no such thing back then in Croatia and Croatia had no previous experience in dealing with matters such as those, no specialised services were operating. What's more, the resources provided for in the budget for that type of activity simply weren't available. All there was was a great amount of enthusiasm among the people. People realized what a tremendous amount of misfortune was occurring all around them and people realized that there were other people who were badly in need of help. That was our infrastructure, especially given the fact that we hardly had anything else that was available to us at the time. We didn't even have a physical office to work in. Croatia was a new country and the cabinet had an office. I moved our office to the seat of the Zagreb Territorial Defence headquarters. It was literally no more than five minutes after they had withdrawn based on an agreement to leave Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What period are we talking about? We know that Vukovar fell sometime in November 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I am talking about that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when Vukovar fell can you give us an impression as to how much of Croatia, if any of it at that time, was occupied by any foreign forces? And by "foreign," I mean JNA because in this instance we are essentially -- for all intents and purposes, we have the internationally recognised boundaries of Croatia. So could you tell us at that point in time when the office is established.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Croatia had actually not been recognised by this time, it took another month or two. Nevertheless, about one-third of Croatia's territory was already under occupation, more or less about one-third I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you have an approximation as to how many displaced persons existed at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The figure was fluctuating depending on what exactly was going on, but normally it would be between 200.000 and 300.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is after the fall of Vukovar we're talking about. I'm talking November 1991, November/December, that period, when you're establishing the office.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Before that period, during that period, and after that period. I'm talking about 1991 and the first half of 1992. 200.000 to 300.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you told us that Croatia did not have the sort of technical knowledge, in fact you've indicated that there was a lack of sophistication in understanding the difference between refugee and displaced person. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how much technical assistance came from the international community, the UN, neighbouring countries, countries that had been engaged in assisting other places with these sorts of humanitarian crisis. How much of that came in in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Nothing. All we received was a letter from Geneva to the effect that aid had been dispatched to the UNHCR Belgrade mission. They said their plan was to give 28 per cent of the overall aid contained in that shipment to Croatia, that being Croatia's territorial share in Yugoslavia as a whole at that time. I suppose that was what the calculation was based on; however, we were unable to travel to Belgrade at the time because all the roads were blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just, I guess, cut to the quick on this one. At this point, as I understand it, Croatia's being attacked by the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Headquarters of JNA, for all intents and purposes I'm talking about the main headquarters, are in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's perceived that that Yugoslav, Serbian, whatever you want to call it, government is the one that's actually attacking Croatia and now you have these folks in Geneva writing a letter to Croatia saying, Go to Belgrade to collect your 28 per cent of aid. Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I think that's what happened. At first I don't think they were aware of what exactly was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did they ever send anybody to become aware? Because you're talking about 200, 300.000 displaced persons. Presumably the UNHCR is interested. The international community must have been interested. The neighbouring countries must have been interested. When was the first time, to your knowledge, did they come in with technical and perhaps even other sorts of assistance, financial assistance, to help with this humanitarian situation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The first delegations to arrive in Zagreb were so-called high-ranking delegations. It was splendid to welcome people such as Cyrus Vance, Herbert Okun, and other high-ranking officials, international officials. Nevertheless, they wouldn't go any farther than the political level, what I might term the political level. It took months for the first UNHCR delegations to start arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when they did arrive, what exactly did they provide as far as assistance?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: When they arrived, they struck me as being similar to myself several months before in terms of the fact that they had no office, no premises to use, they had no idea where they had just landed, and they had no idea at all what was going on around them. It took them a while to set up an office to use, set up their equipment, and set up their teams. Throughout this humanitarian crisis in Croatia, if we consider the figures, the UNHCR or any other international organizations, were providing assistance. Despite this, if you look at the monthly breakdown of all the aid they provided, this never exceeded a measly 11 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, but let me focus you again. I'm going to ask you to maybe pick up the speed of your answers, slightly that is. When they first arrived, you indicated that they didn't have an office space, they didn't have a place to put their equipment. I take it at some point they did become oriented, they did set up an office, and they did start providing some assistance. Can you please tell us as far as technical assistance, know-how, that is, what sort of assistance did they provide initially?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The first assistance we received or the first cooperation we had with them was cooperation with regard to the establishment of a database that we got based on the list of all displaced persons and refugees who at the time were in Croatia. The UNHCR suggested we do that. They gave us the equipment and the funds to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What was the purpose of having this database, as far as you understand?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: We needed to know who was who, where they had come from, or from which place they had been driven out, how old they were, how many children there were, how many sick people, where they were. We had to know their needs and how to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. First of all, what period are we speaking about? When is the first database established?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge at that point in time is there some sort of a line item in the budget of the Republic of Croatia to take care of your office's needs?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The amounts that were received from government were received in an irregular fashion. The only two persons that were receiving a salary in the first three or four months were the head of that office and myself. Everybody else volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me stop you. We will hear later on that you became a member of the parliament, and as you well know normally once a year there's a -- there are discussions about a budget. So that way the government can plan its expenditures, you know, over the year. So my question was, and I would ask you to specifically answer my question: Was there a budget set aside by the government for these needs to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what the amount was?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say now because we had a different currency at the time, which later on was converted into the new currency. But the government covered the costs for organized accommodation, schooling, medical treatment, and for all other needs of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to this database, just a couple of quick questions before we move on unless the Trial Chamber has some questions. First, was the database ever used for discriminatory purposes? In other words, you know -- you can identify exactly how many of one particular group are coming, where they're coming from, that way you can then later on discriminate against them, provide them with no education, no proper accommodation, maybe direct them in places where they would be abused. Do you know whether that was one of the purposes or whether the database was used in any way in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: We did not use the database for any discriminatory purposes. We needed it for the technical implementation of our work. We had to know where we had people and how many; we had to know their needs. It was necessary for us to know where they had come from because at any given moment we wanted to be able to return those people to the places of their origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you, was this database -- I know you took a census essentially initially, was this database updated; and if so, how often was it updated?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It was updated periodically. New arrivals were registered, and those who had left were deleted from the register. The database was often used for the needs of humanitarian organizations, especially for the International Red Cross and their search programmes and for the programmes of putting together family members because many families had been split by the war. And when those people became refugees they looked for each other and it was much easier to find them using our data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And can I -- from your answer, am I correct in assuming that that database was shared with the international organizations?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if UNHCR, for instance, wanted to have access to it so it could -- for its own purposes, they would have access to it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very quickly, how was the data collected?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: We had people who worked in the local centres where the displaced persons and refugees had been put up, and they entered the necessary data in the forms provided. Later that data was collected to become part of the central base and there the data was processed. It was archived, backed up, and whatever needs to be done with such a base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated local centres, so perhaps it would be good at this point to inform us exactly how was this entire network set up, that is, the network with respect to your particular office? Because we know that you were asked to create an office, I assume that was in Zagreb, but now you mentioned local centres. So could you give us a few words on how it was set up?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In all administrative units called municipalities in -- as they were called in former Yugoslavia, there was so-called social welfare centres. As our resources were limited, we felt we had to focus on priority issues. The social welfare centres worked with addicts, poor families, and others. We suggested that these centres become part of the structure of our office, and the government approved of that, because the most important social issue in Croatia at the time was taking care of over half a million refugees and displaced persons. At that moment that was about 12 per cent of the overall population and the territory of the country was effectively reduced by one-third. You can draw your own conclusions out of these facts. So the social welfare centres became the local offices of the government centre for displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Above that level, above -- so you have -- at the very bottom you have local centres. What's at the next step?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The next higher level was the level of regional centres. They were organized on functional principles, but there a distribution did not correspond to the administrative breakdown of the country, that is, regions and counties which were in place at the time in Croatia. So on the territory of one county or region there could be more than one territorial offices, due to the fact that there was such a huge number of displaced persons and refugees. That was the case in Split, for example, which with the surrounding territory is one Croatian county but we had three or four regional offices there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was that because of the numbers of refugees and displaced persons and the numbers of various local centres?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to set up as many reception centres as possible in places where refugees and displaced persons arrived in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you briefly tell us how many are we speaking of, reception centres ultimately in places where people are placed, where they are displaced or refugees, so we have some sort of an understanding of the numbers that we're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In Croatia there were exactly 597 official sites -- reception sites; thus, we took care and provided for about half the displaced persons and refugees and the other half took care of themselves. They found accommodation with relatives, friends, or simply people who had taken them up. But after some time even those families turned to us to cover the cost of the accommodation of those refugees and displaced persons. From time to time, the displaced persons and refugees constructed their own accommodation. If the conditions were such that they could continue living there, then we tolerated that and legalised them; but most times, as there were -- as there was no infrastructure, there were no hygienic conditions, et cetera, such places had to be shut down and evacuated. And we then moved those people to other more suitable places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, sticking with that, can you just give us one example so that we have an understanding of what we're talking about, where you had some refugees or displaced persons setting up their own accommodations and where eventually they have to be moved because of a variety of reasons, one being hygienic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In big cities you can always find empty premises such as provisional accommodation for construction workers and the like, and people simply entered those premises and tried to organize their lives. There were such settlements without electricity, without running water, without sewage. We either tried to provide them with the necessary infrastructure or, if that was not possible, we strove to move the people to other facilities. There were many examples. I was busy doing that practically around-the-clock for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There were other cases, some of them dramatic, when the police or somebody would call you up, saying that on the central railroad station there were two trains full of women and children waiting for a day or two there and who didn't know where to go, and many of who refused to get off the train before they were told where they would be put up. The worst case being if you had two or three people on such trains who couldn't move or who had to -- or who were in need of urgent medical treatment within hours or they would die. We had such occurrences in Zagreb, Osijek, and other Croatian towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to go into some more specifics, and before I do that maybe it might be good to ask you one question before I go into your background a little bit more because we do have some documents here. But just so we understand, did -- when the refugees and displaced persons began arriving, did they give you any advance notice and what sort of numbers are we talking about? Because I think it might be good for this Trial Chamber to understand that while Croatia is one-third occupied, fighting a war - and I'll be asking where the front line is - to really truly understand what sort of numbers we're talking about in the periods of advanced notice that you had in order to take care of these sorts of individuals, displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about 1991, 1992, and 1993. The numbers of displaced persons and refugees in that period - and I'm talking about people permanently accommodated in Croatia - the numbers ranged and 500.000 to 700.000 people, which means that we worked with at least a million persons because some of them moved on and some of them were fortunate enough to be able to return. Some of them died, unfortunately. But that number was always over 500.000 from 1991 through 1993. Zagreb airport at the time was only 25 kilometres away from the front line. The front line was not far from Zagreb. Sisak is only 60 kilometres away. Karlovac is 40 kilometres from Zagreb, and the front line ran through the outskirts of Karlovac. Croatia is a small country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But how much advanced notice did you get? Did they say, for instance, in one week so many refugees, displaced persons, are coming so you can at least get the places ready and food there and the water? How much advanced notice?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There was no advance notice because we're talking about people who were persecuted. In individual cases we may have received advance notice. Mostly we learned from the media that people were crossing lines, crossing the line, but we mostly learned of their presence only after they had already arrived. No preparation was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What sort of numbers are we talking about? I'm talking about at one given time when you have a wave of refugees, of displaced persons, coming in, not the overall numbers.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Exact figures can be found in the documents. I said that the numbers never fell under 500.000. I can tell you that on one weekend 50 or 60.000 people arrived in Zagreb. When these 60.000 people go to see a football match, that is a logistical problem; but if these people are refugees, that's a huge problem. There were two such incidents, and on a few occasions it was similar in Split. There were two principal migration lines in Croatia, one in the north and the other in the south. People from Bosnia-Herzegovina mostly arrived in Split first, and those heading north mostly arrived in Zagreb first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to where we started so we have some dates about your particular involvement. You indicated sometime in 1991 you got involved. Could you just briefly tell us before we get to the documents, you know, when -- at what period were you working with displaced persons and refugees and what positions you held.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I was the secretary-general of that office from its establishment in November 1991 till March or April 1993, when I was elected to Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long did you serve in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While you were in the parliament, did you continue in any way to be involved in the matters in which you had been involved, that is, with displaced persons and refugees; and if yes, how so?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved. It was my wish to stay involved because once you experience something like that, being a member of parliament is a very boring job. I remained active in the humanitarian field and I organized several convoys in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and often I too travelled with these convoys in both countries. I didn't take so much interest in debates about laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: So that toward the end of my term in office I decided to return to that office. I accepted Dr. Granic's invitation and returned to the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What period are we speaking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Late 1995 and 1996. I returned to work to the same Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just very quickly so we can get this into the record, if I can show you some documents. 1D 02642. It should be the first document in your bundle, 2642. We see here this is a decision to appoint you secretary-general, it says Damir Zoric, 13 November 1992, and this is to the office of displaced persons and refugees. My first question is: You indicated that you worked in 1991, but here we see that it's not until 13 November 1992 that you're actually appointed officially with this decision. Can you give some sort of an explanation, and make it brief and quickly.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: What we're looking at here is the creation of a new government. The prime minister wanted me to remain in that position. The previous government, however, the one that had first set up my office, Dr. Greguric's cabinet, that is the cabinet that we're talking about when we talk about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document, and that is 1D 02640, 2640. Here we see 5 March 1993, we see your name again, and this is the decision to relieve you. Am I to understand that this decision is based on you being a member of parliament or having to do with you being elected?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I can't see the decision, but, yes, I had to leave my position because it was simply incompatible for me to remain in an executive position and also to be part of the legislative body at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Zoric, your package should have been done with exact precision. The numbers are there, so if you have a problem let us know. We have duplicates. You don't need to be fishing around in the back. They're all in the sequential order of what I'm going now. All right. 1D 02643, 2643. This is another decision. This is to appoint as deputy head of the office of displaced persons, and here we have 23 November 1995. My first question is: Are you still a member of the parliament at this point, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you the next question. Now, can you please explain how is it that you are a member of the parliament and at the same time you are appointed as deputy head of the office? They seem to be somewhat incompatible. Brief explanation very quickly because we have a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The position of the president was incompatible, not that of the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: That is precisely why I was appointed deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And very briefly if you could just tell us, what did that job entail? What were your responsibilities while you were the deputy head? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I was preparing to replace Dr. Rebic as head of office. It was on account of poor health that he was minded to leave the office and the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go to the next document, 1D 02639, 2639, we see that this is a decision, it's dated 22 February 1996. We see your name, and this is a decision to appoint president, deputy president, and members of the steering council of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. And we see that you're being appointed. Can you give an explanation as to what exactly this is?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: This is the steering council, the committee. It was appointed by the government from the ranks of cabinet members, MOPs, humanitarian workers, and people who were actually employees of this particular body. So this council monitored the work of the body itself. The other members of that steering council or committee were one or two MPs, another one was the president of Karitas. I was there on behalf of the office's employees. Dr. Kostovic was there on behalf of the cabinet, and so on and so forth. This was a body that monitored and steered, in a manner of speaking, the work of this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go to the next document, 1D 02639, 2639, this is 22 February -- oh, did we? Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, you're absolutely right. 2641, 2641, and this is 3 May 1996. And we see here this is a decision to appoint you as head of office. We also note by your name MA, I suppose that's masters, you have yet to receive your Ph.D. at this point. Could you please tell us, what is this position now and who are you replacing?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I replaced Dr. Rebic. I was now to all practical intents the head of that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, since we mentioned Dr. Rebic, let's get this out of the way? Who is Dr. Rebic because there have been some insinuations by one of the witnesses of the Prosecution that he was part of or engaged in activities related to the Prosecution's allegations of a joint criminal enterprise with respect to the Republic of Croatia and the events that were occurring in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I have the transcript ready here if we need to look at it, but who is Dr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Dr. Adalbert Rebic is a person who is held in high regard, both in Zagreb and throughout Croatia. He was asked to become head of office. He teaches at the university, he teaches theology. His subject is called biblical archaeology, exegesis, and he also teaches Hebrew. He is one of Croatia's foremost experts on Israel and the Hebrew language. He, as a matter of fact, speaks four or five different languages. He speaks ancient Hebrew, I think he even speaks Aramaic, Greek, Latin, so on and so forth. He is a highly educated person, an erudite. I think he wrote over 20 or 30 books on the subjects that he deals with professionally. The cabinet wanted him to head the office precisely because he was a person of high moral standards. The cabinet believed that this would be some form of a guarantee to all potential donors. That is how we made it through the war, because of donations. Dr. Rebic would be able to guarantee by his reputation that no funds would be embezzled and that no humanitarian aid would end up being misused. His duty was to head the office, to represent the office, to work with international organizations, to motivate people. My duty, on the other hand, was to get people organized. My job was more hands-on. Regardless of this, we weren't very fussy, we all did everything. It really depended on the circumstances, and the same principle applied to Dr. Rebic. I think Dr. Rebic first got a car that he could use late in 1993, and this was a gift from some Munich-based organization.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to get into those specifics. I just wanted to know who he is. Now, as I understand it from your answer, he's number one and you're number two?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I'm just saying this to show that Dr. Rebic was a very modest person, a simple person, and that's why I mentioned that. Yes, he was the number one man and I was the number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And how was the division of labour? You touched on it briefly, but tell us exactly so we know what Dr. Rebic is doing and what you're doing. And I'm speaking about when you're the secretary-general and he's the head of the office, and very briefly and very quickly.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: My responsibility was to track down people, to find places, to make sure that all the bills were paid, to get people organized, and to provide guidance. What you call distribution of labour was not always possible. He sometimes did my job and I sometimes took over from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But what was his job concretely?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: He was the head of office. He was the number one man. He liaised with the cabinet, with international organizations, and he was the public face of the office, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it we're taking a break at 9.30? Okay. Very well -- 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very quickly let's get two documents out of the way so then we can move on to more substantive documents. The one is 1D 02915, 2915. And if you don't have it we'll provide it for you, but I see this is a certificate of appreciation. It's dated 9 January 1993. And could you please tell us a little bit about this, what is it, why did you receive it, and why is it -- what can we glean from this? Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: We were being approached throughout by many organizations and individuals from both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina with requests for assistance. The first thing they always asked for was food because that was about all we could provide, foodstuffs, clothing, firewood, that sort of thing. I received several thank-you notes such as this one. People obviously came to me for material assistance, and I did what I could. What we're looking at here is the BH army command, specifically Maglaj municipality, which is somewhere north of Zenica and south of Derventa. It's signed by two commanders Anto Marincic and Sulejman Herceg. Obviously this is a joint command with Croat and Bosnian Muslim forces fighting jointly in that particular municipality. This means that our aid made it far into Bosnia, and we're looking at early January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I think if we look at the original document on the left side we see the coat of arms of the Armija of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do we see that, the original, the B/C/S version? Top left side.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I do have a copy and I can see the coat of arms you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document 1D 02916, this is now dated 9 June 2005, and we see it's from the head of municipality of Travnik. Could you please tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: My apologies, I can't see the document for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll get it for you very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could have some assistance from the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us what this is about, and it says something about ambassador. You may want to have your glasses handy because we're going to be going through some documents. Every second counts.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the meantime I had spent two years in Sarajevo as ambassador. I received this charter in the city of Travnik in 1995 [as interpreted]. I had been pursuing my private business interests for several years before this, and I had not been involved in any public activity, despite which Travnik municipality awarded me freedom of the city of Travnik. I was pleasantly surprised when I received this. They said at the time that this was an expression of gratitude for all the help I had offered them during and after the war. I was one of those people who were making an effort to stop the clashes between Croats and Bosniaks in Central Bosnia. Travnik is a municipality with a clear Bosniak majority. As to this decision, I actually attended the assembly meeting when the decision was taken by a unanimous vote of all the local deputies. Thus, the decision was signed by the Travnik mayor, Tahir Lendo. There is nothing else that is really peculiar about this charter. I am, however, pleased to have been awarded freedom of the city, especially such a city as Travnik. I was awarded this at a time when I had for several years already not been involved in politics at all. A full seven years after I had last held any sort of official position or acted as a state official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we can see from line 16 on page 27 that it says 1995, actually it's 2005, correct, when you received this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for the record, could you please tell us when you were ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia's ambassador, that is, to BiH, when, what period?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: From 1999 to 2000, the end of 2000, November 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the person that signed this particular document, by looking at his name can you tell us whether he's a Croat, a Bosniak, or a Serb just by looking at the name or do you know the person; if so, what is he?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I hadn't met him before this time. He's obviously a Bosniak because the name is Muslim. I'm not sure about his affiliations, but I would assume that he's a Bosniak. Travnik is predominantly Bosniak. This is the very heart of all Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It's an old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be a good time for me to break, so if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question for the witness. Witness, I'm reading this document. Could you give me a clarification in respect to the meaning of the second paragraph of this document. This document was drafted in 2005, and we could conclude that you are being thanked for having assisted the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an ambassador. But in the second paragraph I see that mention is made to what you did as a statesman, peacemaker, politician, humanist, there's also reference to your government, but during the war and not in the year 2000, the year 1999 or 2005. So what did they mean exactly by this second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they probably meant my contribution in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. I'm less certain about the figures of speech they decided to use for the purposes of wording this charter. I'm not sure what exactly they had in mind; it's difficult for me to say. I do, however, know that the municipal council had to cast a vote on this. They invited me to the session, they proposed this decision, and there was unanimous acceptance for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously the gentleman's quite modest and I think we'll -- throughout the testimony we'll see exactly why such an award was given to him through his efforts during the relevant period. But with that I would ask that we take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed, please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get to the documents so I'm going to direct your attention to 1D 02623, 2623. You don't have to start from the beginning, we're going to go to the very next document, 2623. Do you have it? This is a decree we see that it's dated 30th of August, 1991, and could you please comment on this particular document. First of all, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it, it's a decree of the Government of the Republic of Croatia on the establishment of the Office for Refugees of the Republic of Croatia. I see that here the term refugees is still used even though this office was actually established for the needs of displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: These were the first attempts to establish a coordinating body in Croatia to take care of the people who were expelled from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we -- if I could direct your attention to Article 11, at that point in time you see Article -- or some general, minimum rules for the organizing of the living and work of refugees and we see that. Let me ask you this question: With respect to -- what do we mean by health and social adaptation? To your understanding, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I believe this is meant to mean that displaced persons should by no means be excluded from society. Apart from a minimum subsistence they should get from the state, from our office, such as accommodation and food, they should be enabled to participate in social activities such as enjoy education and enjoy all other rights as all other citizens do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, in Article 11 we also see that ensured schooling for children. And my question is: Do you know whether additional schools were built or whether additional classrooms were established, additional teachers were hired to absorb the needs of the displaced persons at that point in time? We're speaking 1991.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: At that time we could not establish new schools. All children that were at the age when they should go to school were included in existing classes, in existing schools up to the maximum numbers possible. We tried to respect what we call pedagogical standards. But even so, we had not 20 students per classroom but 40, say. Teachers who were also displaced themselves were invited to take part in these activities in schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just very briefly, Article 12 we see that this is published in the Official Gazette. Am I to understand -- are we to understand that this along with the other legislation as we've received, was available for all, including the international organizations such as UNHCR to see exactly what the legislation was in place dealing with refugees and displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe earlier you had mentioned a Mr. Greguric, and so -- because you had indicated when I showed you the first document when you were appointed, which was in 1992, and you indicated that you had actually began working under this particular government. We see here President Dr. Franjo Greguric -- this is the individual that you're talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was prime minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Two small things I wanted to raise with the witness. Indeed this office has been mentioned by other witnesses who spoke about this and there were a number of questions that had remained unanswered. Since we have the secretary-general of this office we may as well ask a few questions of him as to the way the office operated. Article 1, Witness, we can see the make-up of this office, representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, of Defence, et cetera. Under number 8, I see Croatian Red Cross. Could you enlighten us on this. Could you tell us whether the Croatian Red Cross took part in work meetings with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're speaking about an office established in August 1991, and it was active for about three months. That office could not provide for all needs, so another office was established called the government Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. And I was secretary-general of that office. But I can answer your question, yes, the Red Cross participated very actively in taking care of displaced persons. In fact, they were the only organized structure that had been present from earlier times. They even had some facilities that were previously used for summer schools and similar purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at Article 3. In this decree law, this office is supposed to cooperate with the UNHCR from Geneva. As far as you know, were there connections, links, meetings, working meetings, were there continuous follow-up so that the UNHCR could be informed of anything that may have happened later on with regard to the arrival of refugees into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no cooperation on a regular basis at the time, and the UNHCR had not yet come to Croatia. We tried to inform them in writing of the events in Croatia. It is telling that this article reads: " ... the UNHCR ... in Geneva," because they should have been in Croatia but they weren't. So we speak of the UNHCR in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But rather later on when you took up office, did you have close links with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I took over the office and when the representatives arrived in Croatia, I had good cooperation with the representatives of UNHCR. During my term in office from 1991 till 1993, the UNHCR had three high representatives and I cooperated very well with all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas -- one moment, I believe there is another question by a Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, sorry for interrupting you. Witness, I would like to follow-up on the President's question. You said that you cooperated with the UNHCR in Geneva; however, at the beginning of the hearing you said that the word "refugees," which can be found in this document, was wrongly used because you took care of internally displaced persons, so displaced in their own country, that is, Croatia. Therefore, with regard to your cooperation with the UNHCR in Geneva, what level was it at because you, you were supposed to look after Croats who were displaced in their own country whilst the UNHCR, as far as I can see, was supposed to take care of individuals coming from other countries and who found themselves in Croatia. It is true that today the issue of internally displaced persons is a question that is now part of the remit of the UNHCR. There is a debate as to whether the UNHCR should look after internally displaced people or not, but that is a question raised today. But back then I think that the policy of the UNHCR was to look after refugees. So what kind of cooperation did you enjoy with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I understood you, Your Honours, but I must say that apart from displaced persons, that is, Croatian citizens who were put up in Croatia, some of them found accommodation in third countries. Some Croatian displaced persons were -- or rather, found accommodation in Hungary so that they actually became refugees. Some found accommodation in Austria, some in Germany, and a smaller number in Slovenia, so that some of our citizens did have the status of refugees. I believe this was a natural development as the governments of those countries suggested to us that we should work more closely, cooperate more closely, with the UNHCR. The office considered its mandate whether we should also deal with displaced persons and refugees so that talking about the humanitarian crisis in former Yugoslavia at international level it was decided that -- to give us a mandate for such issues too. Throughout my work, I cooperated well with the UNHCR. Our work, or rather, in our work we were not so much concerned with legal or formal issues, but our major concern was the alleviation of the humanitarian crisis. We had to prevent a catastrophe because people in -- the number of people in exile, wherever they had come from, was growing rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. This concept of refugees and displaced persons, let me take the example of an individual who is displaced and, say, arrives in Zagreb and is going to be looked after by the office in charge of his situation. This individual may spend some time in Croatia and then leave for a third country, say in Norway. In Norway that person is going to enjoy the status of a refugee. Did you take care of this type of situation in a very specific and precise way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were such situations, but I repeat, initially all people who had been expelled, driven out of their homes, or who had left their homes in any fashion, we called them refugees. In Croatian and other Slavic languages, that word means a person who for some reason flees due to the existence of threat to their lives. Only later did the UNHCR point out to us that in international terminology the -- there is a distinction between refugee and displaced person. The Croatian word "prognanik," probably would be better translated into English as "expellee" than displaced person. But when the new office became active and when the new decree on the status of these people was passed, we tried to adhere to international terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you're going into semantics mentioning, for instance, the word expellee, line 24, page 35. What you say is interesting; however, I guess there are situations in which individuals are displaced or refugees although they were not expelled because they decided to find themselves in such situations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such persons. There were persons who arrived because they feared for their lives, and fear is a very subjective notion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've come across this type of situation, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just sticking with this topic just a couple of quick questions. I know that it was pointed out to you by the UNHCR that there is a legal distinction between a -- somebody who is displaced and a refugee. But factually speaking, as far as the treatment, the way those two were treated, a displaced person versus a refugee, were there any differences in that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're going to get into more documents at some point, but as far as placement was concerned were there any distinctions being made that displaced persons should go to certain centres and refugees should go to other centres?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No, that was not our position. We were happy to find accommodation, whatever -- of whatever type. But in the first year Croatia mostly received persons who we would call displaced, and only after the start of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina we saw a significant -- the arrival of a significant number of refugees to Croatia. So we filled all existing facilities, but once they were full we had to look for additional ones or construct additional ones so that in the second half of 1992 and in 1993 there were many facilities with refugees only because they arrived later. And in the facilities that had existed previously we put up displaced persons because they arrived earlier. One of the problems that we faced was that many facilities for social welfare were of seasonal type, which means that they couldn't be used in winter-time. Tourist facilities on the coast mostly lack heating because those are facilities for staying in summer-time only. But in the situation we were you must provide accommodation to people so that they can survive the winter there also. None of us ever dreamed that it would take so long. We all thought that within months or within a year at the most we would be able to return those people to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- since we're on this topic very briefly, let me just go in a different direction from my planned direct. Were there possibilities and did it occur where refugees or displaced persons who were, for instance, initially registered in one centre and then made arrangements either on their own or through the authorities to be transferred or relocated to other centres; and if that occurred, can you give us an explanation as to why it would have happened?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: There were such cases initially due to the programmes of putting together families. Members of one family could be found in different cities, and we tried to bring them all together at one place so that -- the consequence of that was a vacancy and those vacancies were filled. So there was some amount of relocation. Some facilities could not be used for longer than a few months because the conditions were unsatisfactory. Sometimes the government would pay for the necessary adaptation, and we were building three or four large accommodation facilities and we located them in such a way that -- in such a way as to enable people to be relocated to a place closer to their original home. We called that closer to home. We considered it better for people to be closer to their regions of origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Because we wanted them to return to their homes, because their life would have been more bearable and easier in their natural environment. So the displaced persons from Vukovar who found accommodation on the coast and wanted -- wanted to be relocated to Slavonia, for example, we gave them the possibility to be closer to their town. We built those facilities with the assistance of the German government which had sent a specialised agency to build those accommodation facilities. Apart from the Germans, the Turkish government also provided significant assistance. We tried to equip all those facilities to be used in the winter, which was very demanding from a logistical point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: If I may add, both refugees and displaced persons arrived in greater numbers in spring and summer because at the -- in those seasons there were more massive military operations so that they would arrive then to facilities which were all right for the summer but not suitable for winter-time. The facilities that were impossible to equip for the winter had to be vacated and the people had to be relocated to other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving very quickly, you talked about this census that was taken and the list of tracking of the refugees and displaced persons. Was that in any way used, to your knowledge, as far as family members being able to identify where their other family members were?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was precisely such compounds that made it possible for families to be reunited and for family members to be tracked down. We always tried to gather information as to what the last place of residence was in relation to some people, whether they left Croatia, where they left for, and then we were often in a position to track those people down in other countries. We often came up with very good results precisely thanks to such information that had been collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to this decree that we were on, and that was 2623, 1D 02623, we notice on Article 1 various ministries and you were pointed to the Red Cross, the Croatian Red Cross. Now, before I get to that question, why was it necessary to have all these ministries engaged and to assist in or be part of this office?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the infrastructure that we had wasn't much and very often officials, state officials that we had appealed to for help, wanted to do no more than their job was worth. This decree was binding for a number of state bodies and organizations to each in their own field provide assistance to our office as a specialised agency looking after refugees and displaced persons. We were unable or perhaps to some extent we were able to organize schools to some extent, but not really that well. This decree made it possible for us to go to the education ministry and talk to them about that. Likewise, we asked the health ministry to take charge of health issues. Without this decree any school principal in Croatia could have approached me or any of my assistants, saying that they were under no obligation to take these children onboard because it wasn't exactly clear who would be bearing the costs and now they were under an obligation to take those children in and it was the state who covered all the costs. I think this is actually enshrined in Article 1 of the decree. One thing that I'm certain about is that it did work like this in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back to the Croatian Red Cross, because I think we all have some images as to what Red Cross normally does, can you tell us how the Croatian Red Cross operated, what sort of functions it carried out prior to, say, the conflict, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: If I compare to what I saw before the war, while the former Yugoslavia was still around and if I look at how the Red Cross was functioning back then and if I look at the work of the International Red Cross, the organizations were similar in only name. The Red Cross was an organization that operated on a purely voluntary basis and it was led by a number of, I assume, professionals. And they were gathering blood pools and they organized various courses. They would also collect aid and contributions for families on the brink of society on an annual basis. However, the international HQ soon granted recognition to Croatia's Red Cross and the cooperation that was established was fairly good. Over no more than a short period of time, although they were a small-scale organization to begin with, they grew and became the -- a well-regarded player on the international stage. It was they that set up this tracking service which was of great use to us and we were grateful to them for it. Another important organization at the time was the Karitas. They enjoyed a great deal of credibility at the time and were able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that. Let's go step by step now as opposed to free flow. If we go to the next document, 1D 02637, and I'm going to ask you to keep your answers rather short and to the point so we can move along at a rapid clip. We see that this is a document dated 22 November 1991, it is another decree, it's on the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees. Do you see that, sir? You're shaking your head. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we also see if we go to the last page on Article 12 that this was also published in the Official Gazette; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to pass this decree to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In a way, this decree makes up for some of the shortcomings of the previous one. We see this new office being set up, and if you look at Article 2, you look at all the organizations that there will be some form of cooperation with. You see that the number of the organizations is growing. In addition to Karitas and the Red Cross, you also see the Merhamet organization joining the ranks. At this time we were facing a growing problem with refugees from Bosnia. This is a decree law and any decree law is always published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at Article 4, if you could look at it very quickly and tell us what -- interpret this for us. Because it says: "Surveillance over the work of the office shall be performed by the office's steering council. President and members of the office's steering council shall be appointed and relieved of duty by the Government of the Republic of Croatia ..." and so on. So could you please tell us, what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: It was the head of office that was supposed to run the office and his chief secretary. There was a body in charge of monitoring too, also government appointed, and they were supposed to steer its work, they were supposed to guide its work, and provide guide-lines. This was the steering committee, also to be government appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at Article 5, without commenting on it too much, it appears -- it lists the various offices including Karitas, as you indicated, International Red Cross, and others of which your office is supposed to cooperate with. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Correct. The international organizations at the time wanted to know what this body was, this government body, that they were working with, who was their partner, and that is what this article is for, it specifies who exactly is the partner for any talks or forms of cooperation to international players in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we move to the next document 1D 00902, 00902, dated 5 May 1992, it's a certificate, we see it's signed by Dr. Mate Granic, you told us who he was at the time, and this is a certificate to a Dr. Slobodan Lang. First of all, who is Dr. Slobodan Lang, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dr. Lang. He's a long-time human rights activist and humanitarian worker. He gained a degree of notoriety already during my time as a student, I think it was in Kosovska Mitrovica, he descended into a mine himself as a token of support for the miners who were on strike in Kosovo at the time. He often went to hotspots where we believed human rights of workers and other persons had been violated and he would always go to such areas to offer his support and assistance. He worked at the faculty of medicine and Dr. Granic also taught there. It appears obvious on the face of this document that Dr. Lang was in need of a pass or a certificate that would allow him to go to Croatia's south to see what the situation was like over there as far as the humanitarian situation was concerned. I think he did this job on a professional basis, because I think the subject that he taught was called social medicine. I think he was sufficiently qualified to make an assessment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: -- in this respect, and I think every time he was back from a trip like this he would normally submit a report on what he found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point in time is he associated with any particular ministry?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. At the time, however, there were many people who were willing to help and he was just one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when it's talking about the region of southern Croatia, what region are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: The Adriatic coast, Dalmatia for the most part. In colloquial terms we refer to this region as south Croatia simply because all these areas are actually at Croatia's south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just one final question, please make it very brief. Why would Dr. Lang need a certificate like this? Why can't he just go down there to southern Croatia and do whatever he wanted to do as far as humanitarian assistance is concerned?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: In order for him to reach the coast from Zagreb, I think he would have had to make at least 20 stopovers. When I say "stopovers," I mean various check-points that he'd be pulled over at and he would be requested to declare his identity to prove who he was; otherwise, I don't think he would have been allowed to pass through too many of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 02587, this is May 13, 1992. We see this is a Crisis Staff of the Muslims of Croatia for providing humanitarian and other aid to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a guarantee. We see that it's signed by the Minister of Finance, Jozo Martinovic, and if we look at it very closely we see we're talking in the amount of $30 million US dollars, the then-value as opposed to the value today. Now, could you please tell us, first of all, do you know what is this Crisis Staff of the Muslims of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: I think this is a group of private individuals, well-regarded citizens of Zagreb first and foremost, who came together to set up an association. In keeping with the popular terminology of the time, it was named Crisis Staff. They tried to put together as much equipment, funds, and resources as possible for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, from this am I to understand that this money, 30 million US, at the time is coming out of the budget of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC
utterances.text: If I look at the wording of the document, it appears to be a bank guarantee. Anyone working with money would be happy to be -- to have a document like this available to them, regardless of the value of the dollar right now this is a guarantee that the Ministry of Finance would be paying this sort of money in return for the bills delivered to them. What this is about is the following: There was this Crisis Staff with Croatia's Muslims, and it was for the purposes of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they would be allowed to use up as many as $30 million USD and the Ministry of Finance provided a guarantee that that would be covered. This is as good as a guarantee, and I do have to agree with you that if we think back to Croatia as it was at the time this amount is simply enormous. As a matter of fact, I think even nowadays it could still be seen as an enormous amount of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, just to make sure I understand it with this guarantee because I'm not a banker, never worked in a bank, but it seems to me with this guarantee this organization could go to warehouses, stores, or what have you, and select foodstuffs, medicine, household necessities, and other material to their choosing, to their liking, based on what they believe are the needs, and that -- up to $30 million.
